1a.html:
A pyrometallurgical process applies heat energy to extract or refine a metal. Its advantages:

  1. Reactions become possible. Reactions that are not thermodynamically possible at low temperature become so at high temperature, because \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ; for example carbon reduces most oxides when hot enough.
  2. Easy separation. Molten or vaporised products separate readily from the gangue, for example metal and slag by density, or zinc by distillation.
  3. Fast rates: high temperature gives fast reactions and large throughput.
  4. Cheap energy: carbon is both fuel and reductant, and sulphide oxidation can supply its own heat (autogenous roasting).
pts: Reactions not possible at low temperature become possible at high temperature (with the \Delta G^\circ = \Delta H^\circ - T\Delta S^\circ reason or the carbon example)
Easier physical separation of metal from gangue when the products are melted or vaporised (metal-slag separation)
High reaction rates and large throughput
Cheap carbon as fuel and reductant, or autogenous heat from sulphide oxidation
1a.watch:
• The slide gives the first two advantages; state them first, in its words.
  • Precious metals collected in the molten metal or matte are another valid advantage; disadvantages (fumes, \mathrm{SO_2}, energy for lean ores) are not asked.

1b.html:
Roasting is the heating of an ore or concentrate below its fusion point in excess air, to convert it chemically into a form more suitable for reduction or leaching. Its principal object is to oxidise sulphides to oxides or sulphates, for example 2\,\mathrm{ZnS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\,\mathrm{ZnO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}.

Fluidised-bed roasting. Air is blown up through a grid under a bed of fine concentrate, and the particles are roasted while suspended in the upward gas stream. How the bed behaves depends on the gas velocity:

  1. Fixed bed: at a very low flow the gas permeates the porous bed without disturbing the particles; the pressure drop is proportional to the flow rate.
  2. Expanded bed (AB): as the velocity rises the bed loosens and expands upward; the pressure drop still depends on the velocity.
  3. Lifting point (BC): the pressure drop approaches the weight of the bed per unit area and passes a small peak; the particles are just lifted at the minimum fluidisation velocity.
  4. Fluidised bed (C onward): the pressure drop stays constant, independent of velocity; extra gas bubbles through and the bed flows like a liquid. Roasting is done here: intense mixing, uniform temperature, fast heat and mass transfer; the calcine overflows continuously.
  5. Entrainment: above the particles' terminal velocity they are carried out with the gas (pneumatic transport); the gas velocity is kept below this and cyclones catch the fines.
pts: Defines roasting: heating below the fusion point in excess air to convert the ore to a form suited to reduction or leaching
Principal object (oxidise sulphides to oxides or sulphates) with a balanced reaction
Fluidised-bed roasting: particles roasted while suspended in an upward stream of air through a grid
Stage 1, fixed bed: gas permeates without moving the particles; pressure drop proportional to flow rate
Stage 2, expanded bed: bed expands upward, pressure drop still rises with velocity (AB)
Stage 3, lifting point at the minimum fluidisation velocity; pressure drop reaches the bed weight per unit area (BC)
Stage 4, fluidised bed: pressure drop independent of velocity, bed flows like a liquid; the roasting stage
Stage 5, entrainment (pneumatic transport) above the terminal velocity; particles carried out
1b.watch:
• The slides describe four stages; the fifth, entrainment, is the textbook end of the curve. Some texts split stage 4 into smooth and bubbling beds instead; either set of five earns the marks if each is described.
  • Draw the fluidisation curve with A, B, C and the minimum fluidisation velocity; it carries the stages in one picture.
  • At C it is the pressure drop that stops rising with velocity; the bed still swells a little as bubbles pass.

1c.fix: • Slide 61 writes 3883.3 \mathrm{m^3} for the \mathrm{SO_2} from \mathrm{Cu_2S}; 27\,600 \times 22.4/159 = 3888.3\ \mathrm{m^3}, the value slide 62 adds into its total of 12,135.6 \mathrm{m^3}.
1c.html:
Given: 60 t of matte with 54% FeS; air with 21% \mathrm{O_2} by volume; \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag; the copper blow ends with no excess \mathrm{Cu_2O} or \mathrm{Cu_2S}.

Find: (i) the volume of air to oxidise the FeS, (ii) the total volume of \mathrm{SO_2}, (iii) the mass of slag.

Assumptions: the rest of the matte (46%) is \mathrm{Cu_2S}; 1 t = 1000 kg; gas volumes at STP (0 °C, 1 atm), 22.4 \mathrm{m^3} per kmol. Molar masses: FeS 87.91, \mathrm{Cu_2S} 159.16, FeO 71.85, \mathrm{SiO_2} 60.09 kg/kmol.

Charge.

\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= 0.54 \times 60\,000 = 32\,400\ \mathrm{kg} &\Rightarrow\ n_{\mathrm{FeS}} &= 32\,400/87.91 = 368.6\ \mathrm{kmol} \\ m_{\mathrm{Cu_2S}} &= 0.46 \times 60\,000 = 27\,600\ \mathrm{kg} &\Rightarrow\ n_{\mathrm{Cu_2S}} &= 27\,600/159.16 = 173.4\ \mathrm{kmol} \end{aligned}

(i) Air for the FeS (slag blow)

2\,\mathrm{FeS} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} = 2\,\mathrm{FeO} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2}
\begin{aligned} n_{\mathrm{O_2}} &= \tfrac{3}{2}(368.6) = 552.8\ \mathrm{kmol}, \qquad V_{\mathrm{O_2}} = 552.8 \times 22.4 = 12\,380\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\text{air}} &= \frac{12\,380}{0.21} = 58\,970\ \mathrm{m^3} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} of air at STP.

(ii) Total SO2

The copper blow oxidises part of the \mathrm{Cu_2S}, and the \mathrm{Cu_2O} then reacts with the rest:

\begin{aligned} 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\,\mathrm{O_2} &= 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\,\mathrm{SO_2} \\ 2\,\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} &= 6\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2} \\ \text{sum (divided by 3):}\quad \mathrm{Cu_2S} + \mathrm{O_2} &= 2\,\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2} \end{aligned}

With nothing left over, one-third of the \mathrm{Cu_2S} is oxidised to \mathrm{Cu_2O}, and each kmol of \mathrm{Cu_2S} gives 1 kmol of \mathrm{SO_2}; each kmol of FeS also gives 1 kmol.

\begin{aligned} V_{\mathrm{SO_2}}(\mathrm{FeS}) &= 368.6 \times 22.4 = 8\,256\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\mathrm{SO_2}}(\mathrm{Cu_2S}) &= 173.4 \times 22.4 = 3\,884\ \mathrm{m^3} \\ V_{\mathrm{SO_2}} &= 8\,256 + 3\,884 = 12\,140\ \mathrm{m^3} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 1.21\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} of \mathrm{SO_2} at STP (542 kmol).

(iii) Slag

\mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}\qquad (71.85 + 60.09 = 131.94\ \mathrm{kg/kmol})
\begin{aligned} m_{\mathrm{FeO}} &= 368.6 \times 71.85 = 26\,480\ \mathrm{kg}, \qquad m_{\mathrm{SiO_2}} = 368.6 \times 60.09 = 22\,150\ \mathrm{kg} \\ m_{\text{slag}} &= 368.6 \times 131.94 = 48\,630\ \mathrm{kg} \end{aligned}

Answer: about 48.6 t of \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2} slag.
pts: (i) Splits the charge into 32,400 kg FeS and 27,600 kg \mathrm{Cu_2S} (368.6 kmol FeS)
(i) Balanced reaction 2\mathrm{FeS} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{FeO} + 2\mathrm{SO_2}, so 1.5 kmol \mathrm{O_2} per kmol FeS
(i) \mathrm{O_2} needed about 12,380 \mathrm{m^3} at STP (552.8 kmol)
(i) Air = V_{\mathrm{O_2}}/0.21 \approx 5.90\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} (58,900 to 59,000 \mathrm{m^3} with rounded masses)

(ii) Copper-blow reactions 2\mathrm{Cu_2S} + 3\mathrm{O_2} = 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + 2\mathrm{SO_2} and 2\mathrm{Cu_2O} + \mathrm{Cu_2S} = 6\mathrm{Cu} + \mathrm{SO_2}, giving 1 \mathrm{SO_2} per \mathrm{Cu_2S}
(ii) \mathrm{SO_2} from FeS about 8,250 \mathrm{m^3} and from \mathrm{Cu_2S} about 3,885 \mathrm{m^3}
(ii) Total \mathrm{SO_2} \approx 1.21\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3} at STP (12,135 to 12,150)
(iii) FeO formed about 26,480 kg (26,500 with rounded masses) and the reaction \mathrm{FeO} + \mathrm{SiO_2} = \mathrm{FeO{\cdot}SiO_2}
(iii) \mathrm{SiO_2} taken up about 22,150 kg, or the slag molar mass 131.9 (132) kg/kmol
(iii) Slag about 48.6 t (4.86\times10^{4} kg)
1c.watch:
• Read "60 tons" as metric tonnes, as the course solution does. In short tons (907.2 kg) every answer is 0.907 times smaller, for example about 53,500 \mathrm{m^3} of air.
  • The question gives no temperature for the \mathrm{SO_2}, so quote it at STP. The book version asks for 300 °C and 745 mm Hg: 12\,140 \times (573/273)(760/745) \approx 2.60\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m^3}.
  • Do not divide the \mathrm{SO_2} from the copper blow by 3: the two copper reactions together give one \mathrm{SO_2} for every \mathrm{Cu_2S}, whichever path the sulphur takes.
  • Extra depth: the blister copper is 2 \times 173.4 \times 63.55 \approx 22.0 t, and the copper blow needs another 173.4 kmol \mathrm{O_2}, about 18,500 \mathrm{m^3} of air.

2a.html:
The leaching reagent R reacts at the mineral surface to give a soluble metal species M and other products P. Two situations can arise (see the sketches).

(a) The mineral dissolves completely. All the products are soluble, so the surface simply recedes and no solid layer forms, for example \mathrm{ZnO + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow ZnSO_4 + H_2O}. Across the liquid boundary film the reagent falls from [R]_B in the bulk to [R]_S at the surface, while M and P are highest at the surface and fall to [M]_B and [P]_B. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk of the solution to the mineral-solution interface;
  2. reaction of R with the mineral surface to form the soluble metal species;
  3. diffusion of M (and P) away from the interface into the bulk.

(b) The mineral decomposes and dissolves in parts. An insoluble product, or the undissolved part of the ore, stays behind as a porous residue around the unreacted mineral; leaching goes on only if this layer is porous. Example: \mathrm{CaWO_4(s) + CO_3^{2-} \rightarrow CaCO_3(s) + WO_4^{2-}}. I is the mineral-residue interface and II the residue-solution interface. Kinetic steps:

  1. diffusion of R from the bulk to the residue-solution interface II;
  2. diffusion of R through the porous residue to I;
  3. reaction of R with the mineral at I to form soluble M;
  4. outward diffusion of M and P through the porous layer;
  5. diffusion of M and P from II into the bulk.

Case (a) lacks steps 2 and 4. The slowest step, or a combination, controls the rate.

Accelerating the leaching. Find the rate-controlling step first, then:

  • Film diffusion (steps 1 or 5): stir the solution. The boundary layer thins and the gradients steepen, so the rate rises with stirring speed until it levels off.
  • Chemical reaction (step 3): agitation has no effect. Raise the temperature (activation energy about 10 to 25 kcal/mol, so the rate is very sensitive to it), the reagent concentration (by the reaction order) or the oxidant supply, for example oxygen pressure.
  • Pore diffusion (steps 2 and 4): grind finer, which shortens the path and raises the surface area (10 mm to 0.1 mm gives 100 times the area per unit mass), or roast first to make the solid porous.
  • A higher temperature speeds up all the steps, diffusion only weakly (5 kcal/mol or less).
pts: Sketch (a): mineral, solution and boundary film, with [R] rising from [R]_S to [R]_B and [M], [P] falling from the surface to the bulk
Sketch (b): mineral, porous residue with interfaces I and II, and the [R], [M], [P] profiles across residue and film
Explains situation (a): complete dissolution with soluble products and no solid layer, with an example
Explains situation (b): partial decomposition leaving a porous residue (leaching goes on only if it is porous), with an example
Three steps for (a): diffusion of R in, surface reaction, diffusion of M and P out
Five steps for (b): film diffusion of R, pore diffusion of R, reaction at I, pore diffusion of M and P, film diffusion of M and P
Stirring speeds up leaching when film diffusion (step 1 or 5) controls, but has no effect when the chemical reaction (step 3) controls
Raising the temperature speeds up all steps, the chemical reaction most (activation energy about 10 to 25 kcal/mol against 5 kcal/mol or less for diffusion)
A further method tied to its step: finer grinding (surface area, shorter pore path), higher reagent or oxidant concentration, or roasting to make the solid porous
2a.sketch:
• (a): hatched mineral, solution, liquid boundary film; [R] rising from [R]_S at the surface to [R]_B; [M] and [P] falling from [M]_S, [P]_S to the bulk.
  • (b): mineral, porous residue between interfaces I and II, solution; [R] rising from [R]_I through [R]_{II} to the bulk; [M] and [P] falling from I to II to the bulk.
  • Arrows for R moving in and for M and P moving out, numbered as the kinetic steps.
2a.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 13-17; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 4-5, 13-15
2a.watch:
• The slides number the steps of case (b) 1 to 5 and say "step 1 or step 5" for film diffusion and "step 3" for the reaction; in case (a) these are its steps 1, 3 and 2. Keep your numbering consistent with your sketch.
  • Even when more stirring stops helping, diffusion across the limiting film may still control; the activation energy (diffusion 5 kcal/mol or less, reaction 10 to 25 kcal/mol, that is 21 and 42 to 105 kJ/mol) tells which.
  • Extra depth: for a shrinking particle of radius R_0, the time for complete leaching grows as R_0 under reaction control and as R_0^2 under diffusion through a residue layer, so grinding helps most when pore diffusion controls.

2b.html:
A potential/pH (Pourbaix) diagram shows the thermodynamically stable species of a metal-water system at each potential E and pH, for a chosen ion activity (10^{-3} for leaching), with the water lines drawn on it.

Importance in leaching

  1. Can the mineral be leached at all? The diagram shows the domains where a soluble ion is stable (dissolution) beside those of the solid metal or its oxide. If the system has no soluble species under any conditions, another system (another reagent or a complexing agent) must be examined.
  2. Choice of leaching conditions. The diagram gives the range of pH and potential in which the metal stays in solution. The pH is set with acid or alkali, the potential with an oxidant, a reductant or an external potential. In the Zn-H2O system, zinc and ZnO dissolve as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 (domain A) and as zincate \mathrm{ZnO_2^{2-}} above about 13.4. Leaching of ZnO becomes more efficient the farther the pH is taken below the boundary.
  3. Which cathodic reaction drives the dissolution. Compare the metal's lines with the water lines. Zn lies below both, so it dissolves by hydrogen evolution or oxygen reduction. Cu lies between them, so it needs oxygen or another oxidant. Au lies above both, so it needs a complexing agent such as cyanide.
  4. Recovery. The same diagram shows how to bring the metal out again: raise the pH to precipitate the oxide or hydroxide, or lower the potential (cementation, electrolysis).

Limitations

  1. Sharp lines mislead. A boundary does not mean that all the ions on one side are of one species and all on the other of another; both coexist near the line, which only marks where one species holds the majority.
  2. All major species must be included. Omitting one, for example a complexing ion (\mathrm{CN^-}, \mathrm{NH_3}, \mathrm{Cl^-}) or a sulphur species, can change the diagram dramatically.
  3. No kinetics. Equilibrium data say what can happen, not how fast; rates must be found by experiment on the actual system.
pts: States that the diagram shows the stable species against E and pH, with dissolution (ionic) domains apart from solid domains, so it tells whether a mineral can be leached (if not, another system is examined)
Selection of leaching conditions: pH set by acid or alkali, potential by an oxidant or reductant or an external potential, to enter the dissolution domain
Example with values, such as Zn dissolving as \mathrm{Zn^{2+}} below pH about 6.9 and as zincate above about 13.4, leaching more efficient farther from the boundary
Water lines show the cathodic reaction available: Zn by hydrogen evolution or oxygen, Cu only with oxygen or an oxidant, Au with neither (complexing needed)
A further use, such as recovery by pH change (precipitation) or by lowering the potential (cementation, electrolysis)
Limitation: sharp boundaries do not mean an abrupt change of species; species coexist near a line
Limitation: all major species must be included; omitting one (for example a complexing ion) changes the diagram dramatically
Limitation: equilibrium only, no information on kinetics; rates must be measured by experiment
2b.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 12, 18-30; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 7-11
2b.watch:
• "Discuss the importance" needs an example; the Zn diagram from the slides, with its two dissolution domains, is the quickest one.
  • The water band moves with pH (0 to 1.23 V only at pH 0); compare a metal line with the water line at the same pH.
  • The diagram's activity choice matters: 10^{-6} is usual for corrosion and 10^{-3} for leaching, and lower activities widen the dissolution domains. Each diagram also holds for one temperature (usually 25 degrees C), while real leach liquors are hotter, more concentrated and multi-component; this is a further limitation worth a line.

3a.html:
Percolation (vat or sand) leaching passes the leach solution through a stationary bed of crushed low-grade ore held in large vats or tanks.

Preparation. The ore is crushed to about 5 to 20 mm, large enough for the solution to flow freely through the voids. Fines and clay are removed, because they block the bed; clayey ores do not suit the method.

Procedure.

  1. The ore is loaded into the vats, which are then filled with leaching solution; the solution percolates down through the voids of the bed and is drawn off at the bottom.
  2. After the solution has been in contact with the ore for a set time, it is drawn off and fresh solution is added.
  3. Several stages are needed, run on the counter-current principle in a series of vats, the solution from one vat cycling to the next. The freshest (strongest) solution enters the vat whose ore has been leached longest, and the newest ore meets the weak (spent) solution that has already passed the other vats.
  4. So the particles that are hardest to dissolve meet the strongest solution, while the fresh ore is still readily attacked by the weak one. The solution leaving the fresh-ore vat is the most concentrated pregnant solution, sent to metal recovery.
  5. At each step one vat is being loaded with fresh ore and one is being washed and emptied; then the feed point moves on by one vat (step 1 to step 2 in the sketch).
  6. When its leaching cycle is complete, the ore is washed with water one or more times, to recover the dissolved metal held in the bed, and the leached ore (tailings) is removed.

Performance. With 10 or more leach cycles, 80 to 90% of the metal values are recovered; in the reading's copper example, 90.4% from 1.6% Cu ore with dilute \mathrm{H_2SO_4}. It is a batch process, since vats are idle while charged and emptied, yet it is the most efficient method found for leaching large tonnages of low-grade ore.
pts: Sketch: a series of vats with ore beds and the solution passing from the bottom of one vat to the top of the next
Sketch labels: fresh solution into the most-leached vat, pregnant solution out of the newest-ore vat, vats being loaded and unloaded
Ore crushed to about 5 to 20 mm, with fines and clay removed so the bed stays permeable
Vats filled with solution that percolates through the static bed; after a set contact time it is drawn off and fresh solution added
Counter-current principle: strongest solution to the longest-leached ore, weak (spent) solution to the fresh ore, with the reason
The cycle moves on: one vat loading and one unloading at each step
Washing with water before removal of tailings; 10 or more cycles recover 80 to 90%
Batch process, but the most efficient method for large tonnages of low-grade ore, with an example (copper ore with dilute acid)
3a.sketch:
• A row of vats holding beds of ore covered by solution.
  • Solution path from the bottom of one vat to the top of the next.
  • "Fresh (strong) solution in" at the vat with the most-leached ore; "pregnant solution out" from the vat with the newest ore.
  • One vat "loading fresh ore" and one "unloading leached ore"; a second row showing the next step, with every role moved on by one vat.
3a.src: Hydrometallurgy, slides 39-41; Hydrometallurgy reading (book Ch 5), pp 17-18, 20-21
3a.watch:
• Do not confuse the direction: fresh solution goes to the oldest ore, not to the fresh ore.
  • "Explain how it is carried out" needs the moving sequence of vats; a single tank of ore does not show the counter-current scheme.
  • Percolation is not heap leaching: the ore sits in tanks and is flooded with solution, not sprinkled on a pile.

3b.fix: • The course book (p 34) prints E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.337 - (-440) and \Delta G^\circ = \sim 149.9 kJ/mol: the iron potential is -0.440 V and \Delta G^\circ is negative, -149.9 kJ per mol Fe. Its ratio 4\times10^{-27} follows from a cell of 0.78 V; 0.777 V gives 5\times10^{-27} (either is acceptable).
3b.html:
The metal is won from a clear leach liquor by cementation (contact reduction), gaseous reduction or electrolysis. Cementation is reduction by another metal: a less noble metal (more negative electrode potential) is added, dissolves, and the more noble metal precipitates on its surface.

Principle

For \mathrm{M^{z+} + ze^- = M}, with unit activity of the pure metal,

E = E^\circ + \frac{RT}{zF}\ln a_{\mathrm{M^{z+}}}

The metal with the more negative potential passes into solution and displaces the metal of more positive potential. The series is for 25 C and unit activity, so real concentrations can change the order for metals of close potential.

Mechanism (a corrosion cell)

The precipitant corrodes anodically, and reduction of the noble ion is the cathodic reaction:

\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}\qquad \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}

At first small potential differences on the surface give local cells and the rate is low. Dissolved oxygen (\mathrm{O_2 + 4H^+ + 4e^- \rightarrow 2H_2O}) is reduced preferentially and wastes precipitant, so oxygen is excluded. Once some metal has deposited, it forms a galvanic cell with the precipitant, the whole exposed surface becomes anodic and the rate rises.

Example: copper on scrap iron

\begin{aligned} &\mathrm{CuSO_4 + Fe \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}\\ &E^\circ_{\text{cell}} = 0.337 - (-0.440) = 0.777\ \mathrm{V},\qquad \Delta G^\circ = -2(96485)(0.777) \approx -150\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\\ &a_{\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}}/a_{\mathrm{Fe^{2+}}} \approx 5\times10^{-27}\ \text{at equilibrium} \end{aligned}

So practically all copper can be removed. The liquor runs through long troughs (launders) of scrap steel. Copper forms a curd-like precipitate contaminated with iron residues that must be fire-refined. Iron needed in theory is 55.85/63.55 = 0.88 kg per kg Cu, but acid and ferric ions also consume it:

\mathrm{Fe + H_2SO_4 \rightarrow FeSO_4 + H_2}\qquad \mathrm{Fe + Fe_2(SO_4)_3 \rightarrow 3FeSO_4}

Other uses

  • Gold and silver: zinc dust added to a clarified, de-aerated cyanide solution: \mathrm{2[Au(CN)_2]^- + Zn \rightarrow 2Au + [Zn(CN)_4]^{2-}}.
  • Purification: zinc dust removes Cu and Cd from zinc sulphate electrolyte (\mathrm{Cd^{2+} + Zn \rightarrow Cd + Zn^{2+}}).

The process is simple and cheap and works on dilute solutions, but the product is impure and the precipitant is consumed. It goes faster with a large precipitant area (scrap, dust), good flow past the surface and no oxygen.
pts: Defines cementation: reduction of noble metal ions by a less noble metal that dissolves, the metal depositing on its surface; one of the recovery methods (with gaseous reduction, electrolysis)
Principle: the metal with the more negative reduction potential dissolves and displaces the more positive one; E = E^\circ + (RT/zF)\ln a
The series holds at 25 C and unit activity; concentrations can change the order

Mechanism: precipitant anodic (\mathrm{Fe \rightarrow Fe^{2+} + 2e^-}), noble ion reduced at the cathode (\mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}); local cells first, then a galvanic cell with the deposit
Dissolved oxygen is reduced preferentially and wastes precipitant, so it is excluded
Cu/Fe numbers: cell about 0.78 V, \Delta G^\circ about -150 kJ/mol, equilibrium ratio of order 10^{-27}, so removal is nearly complete
Copper practice: liquor through troughs of scrap iron, \mathrm{CuSO_4 + Fe \rightarrow FeSO_4 + Cu}, curd-like impure cement copper that is fire-refined
Iron consumption: 0.88 kg Fe per kg Cu in theory, more because acid (and ferric ions) also dissolve iron
Gold or silver with zinc dust from de-aerated cyanide solution, with a balanced equation (or zinc dust purification of zinc electrolyte)
Merits and limits or rate factors: simple, cheap, dilute solutions; impure product, precipitant consumed; area, flow, no oxygen

3b.watch:
• No sketch is asked, so none is credited; the figure redraws the slide's corrosion cell.
  • Use one sign convention. With reduction potentials the metal with the more negative potential dissolves; the book's Table 5.1 lists oxidation potentials (signs reversed), which is why its text says "more positive".
  • Gold cementation needs the solution clarified and de-aerated; dissolved oxygen would redissolve gold in cyanide and waste zinc.
  • The same question was set in 2017-18 (3b).

4a.html:
Electrowinning against electrorefining

FeatureElectrowinningElectrorefining
PurposeExtracts metal from a leach liquor (or fused salt)Purifies an impure (crude) metal
Metal sourceMetal ions already in the electrolyteThe impure metal itself, cast as the anode
AnodeInsoluble: Pb-Ag or Pb-Ca-Sn alloy, coated TiSoluble: the crude metal, which dissolves
Anode reaction\mathrm{H_2O \rightarrow \tfrac12 O_2 + 2H^+ + 2e^-}\mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-}
Reversible cell emfLarge (Cu about 0.9 V, Zn about 2.0 V)About zero (same reaction reversed at each electrode)
Cell voltage, energyCu about 2 V, about 2 kWh/kgCu about 0.3 V, about 0.3 kWh/kg
ElectrolyteLoses metal, gains acid; spent electrolyte returns to leachingCu content roughly constant; base impurities build up and are bled
By-products\mathrm{O_2} (acid mist)Anode slime with Au, Ag, Se, Te
ExamplesZn, Cu (SX-EW), Ni, Co, MnCu, Ni, Pb, Ag, Au

In both, the cathode reaction is the same (\mathrm{M^{z+} + z\,e^- \rightarrow M}) and Faraday's law fixes the mass.

Basic conditions for an electrolyte

  1. High ionic conductivity, so the IR drop and energy are low.
  2. High solubility of the metal salt, giving a high metal-ion concentration.
  3. Stability: only the wanted metal is discharged; no volatilisation or hydrolysis.
  4. No attack on the deposit, electrodes or cell; a dense, adherent deposit.
  5. Cheap, easily purified and regenerated (fused salts: low melting point, density different from the metal).
pts: Purpose: electrowinning extracts metal from solution; electrorefining purifies crude metal
Insoluble anode in electrowinning against a soluble crude-metal anode in electrorefining
Anode reactions: oxygen (or chlorine) evolution against metal dissolution
Cell voltage and energy: about 2 V against about 0.3 V for copper, because electrowinning must supply the free energy of decomposition
Electrolyte: depleted in metal and enriched in acid (recycled to leaching) in electrowinning; constant in metal with impurity build-up and bleeding in electrorefining
Electrorefining yields anode slime with precious metals; examples of each process
Electrolyte condition: high conductivity
Electrolyte condition: high solubility of the metal salt
Electrolyte condition: stability, only the wanted metal discharged
Electrolyte condition: no chemical attack on deposit or electrodes
Electrolyte condition: cheap, easily purified, or a fused-salt requirement

4b.html:
Harmful impurities in electrical-grade copper

Electrical copper must conduct about 100 % IACS and draw into fine wire, so impurities are held to parts per million.

  1. Impurities that lower conductivity (dissolved in the copper lattice): P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Ti, Co, Sn, Ni. Even 0.015-0.04 % P (phosphorus-deoxidised copper) cuts the conductivity to about 85 % IACS, against about 101 % for electrolytic tough-pitch copper. Ag, Cd and Zn have little effect.
  2. Impurities that spoil workability and annealing: Bi and Pb (insoluble, segregate to grain boundaries: hot shortness, wire breaks), and Se, Te, S (raise the softening temperature and cause brittleness). Bi is harmful at a few ppm.

Grade 1 cathode allows only about 65 ppm in total, with Bi about 1 ppm and Se, Te about 2 ppm each.

Elimination during electrorefining

Cell: fire-refined anodes (about 99.5 % Cu), pure Cu or stainless-steel cathodes, electrolyte about 40-50 g/L Cu and 150-200 g/L \mathrm{H_2SO_4} at 60-65 ^\circC, 250-350 A/m^2, about 0.3 V. Copper dissolves at the anode and plates at the cathode:

\text{anode: } \mathrm{Cu \rightarrow Cu^{2+} + 2e^-} \qquad \text{cathode: } \mathrm{Cu^{2+} + 2e^- \rightarrow Cu}

The cell potential is too low to dissolve nobler metals or to deposit baser ones, so the impurities separate by potential:

  1. Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt metals) do not dissolve and fall into the anode slime; 30-50 mg/L chloride precipitates any dissolved Ag as AgCl.
  2. Se, Te are present as \mathrm{Cu_2Se}, \mathrm{Cu_2Te}, \mathrm{Ag_2Se}, which are insoluble and go to slime. Pb dissolves and re-precipitates as \mathrm{PbSO_4}; Sn forms an insoluble basic salt; both report to slime.
  3. Base metals (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) dissolve and stay in the electrolyte, since their deposition potentials are far below that of Cu. A bleed stream removes them (Ni as \mathrm{NiSO_4}).
  4. As, Sb, Bi, close to Cu in potential, partly dissolve and partly go to slime. They can co-deposit or form floating slime, so they are held low by the bleed and by liberator cells that electrowin Cu, then As, Sb, Bi from it. Enough dissolved As precipitates Sb and Bi as arsenates.

Keeping the cathode clean: glue and thiourea give a smooth, dense deposit that does not trap slime. The electrolyte is filtered and circulated gently, the current density is kept below the limiting value, and anodes are spaced and aligned. The cathodes (99.99 % Cu) are melted to rod; the slime is treated for Au, Ag, Se, Te.
pts: Names impurities that lower conductivity (P, Fe, Si, As, Sb, Sn, Ni, Co) with an example of the effect (e.g. P-deoxidised Cu about 85 % IACS)
Names impurities that spoil drawability or annealing (Bi, Pb, Se, Te, S), harmful at ppm level
Gives the purity target (cathode about 99.99 % Cu, total impurities a few tens of ppm)
Describes the refining cell: crude anode, cathode, \mathrm{CuSO_4}-\mathrm{H_2SO_4} electrolyte, about 60 ^\circC, about 0.3 V
Electrode reactions and the principle that the small cell voltage separates impurities by potential
Nobler metals (Au, Ag, Pt) do not dissolve and report to the slime (Ag fixed by chloride)
Se and Te as insoluble selenides and tellurides; Pb as \mathrm{PbSO_4} and Sn as basic salt go to slime
Base metals (Ni, Fe, Zn, Co) stay in solution and are removed by bleeding the electrolyte
As, Sb, Bi partly dissolve and can co-deposit or form floating slime; controlled by bleed, liberator cells and arsenate precipitation
Cathode purity practices: addition agents (glue, thiourea), filtration, controlled current density
Slime treated for precious metals and Se, Te; cathodes melted for rod

5a.html:
Mineral: a naturally occurring, solid, crystalline, mostly inorganic compound (or native element) whose composition varies only within narrow limits and whose physical properties are well defined, for example galena (PbS), chalcopyrite (\mathrm{CuFeS_2}) and hematite (\mathrm{Fe_2O_3}).

Ore: a natural aggregate of one or more value minerals and gangue from which a metal can be extracted profitably and conveniently with the technology of the day, for example bauxite for aluminium.

BasisMineralOre
Naturea specific chemical entitya rock: value minerals plus gangue
Deciding testcomposition and crystal structuremetal can be extracted at a profit
Constancyfixed: galena is always galenachanges with price, cost and technology
Relationnot every mineral is an oreevery ore is made of minerals
Exampleclay holds about 20% Al but is not worked for Albauxite is the Al ore

Why the boundary moves. Whether a deposit is ore or only mineralised rock depends on "at a profit", so it moves with economic, technological and legal factors.

  1. Price: if the metal price rises, other things equal, a lower-grade deposit becomes economic; a price fall turns marginal ore back into rock.
  2. Technology: around 1900, ores with less than 1% Pb were not worked; after froth flotation, lead is extracted at a profit from ores with only 0.3% Pb. Rock below 1% Cu was once rejected; today 0.5% Cu rock is processed.
  3. New uses: magnesite used only for refractories was a non-metallic mineral, not an ore; now that it is a source of magnesium it is an ore of Mg.
  4. Access and law: deep-sea manganese nodules are a huge mineral resource but become ore only when deep-sea mining is economic and permitted.

So "mineral" is a scientific term and "ore" an economic one.
pts: Defines a mineral as a naturally occurring, solid, crystalline compound of nearly fixed composition and definite properties, with an example
Defines an ore as an aggregate of value minerals and gangue from which a metal is extracted profitably and conveniently, with an example

States the differences: specific entity against aggregate, chemical against economic test, every ore contains minerals but not every mineral is an ore, with a contrasting example (clay against bauxite, or galena-bearing rock that is not a lead ore)
Explains that the boundary is fixed by profit, so it moves with price, cost, technology and legal factors
Price example: a higher metal price makes a lower-grade deposit an ore
Technology example with numbers: lead ore limit fell from 1% to 0.3% Pb after froth flotation, or Cu from 1% to 0.5%
New-use example: magnesite from refractory mineral to Mg ore (or nodules awaiting deep-sea mining)

  • Coal is not called an ore because no metal is extracted from it.

5b.html:
Advantages of recycling metals (secondary production) over primary production from ore:

  1. Energy saving: scrap is already metallic and needs only melting and refining, not reduction. Savings are about 95% for Al, 85% for Cu, 60-75% for steel and 65% for Pb.
  2. Less CO2 and pollution: CO2 falls by about 90% for Al, 65% for Cu and 50% for steel; primary metallurgy gives about 7-9% of world CO2.
  3. Conservation of resources: less new ore is mined, so the limited high-grade deposits last longer.
  4. Fewer, simpler operations: no mining, ore dressing, roasting or smelting, so the metal is cheaper for the producer.
  5. Land and water: no open-pit mine or hazardous tailings, and much less water than mineral processing or hydrometallurgy.
  6. Less waste: end-of-life products go back into the closed loop instead of to landfill.
  7. Supply security: urban mining recovers critical metals (Li, Co, rare earths) locally and cuts dependence on imports.
pts: Energy saving because scrap is already metallic (only melting and refining), with numbers such as 95% Al, 85% Cu, 60-75% steel
Lower CO2 and pollution, with a number (CO2 cut about 90% Al, 65% Cu, 50% steel, or primary metal 7-9% of world CO2)
Conservation of resources: limited high-grade ore preserved
Fewer and simpler operations, so cheaper metal
No mine or tailings and less water
Less waste to landfill (closed-loop cycle)
Supply security: urban mining of critical metals such as Li, Co and rare earths

5c.html:
1. Alloys are recycled as alloys. Obsolete scrap is mostly alloy, and refining it to pure metal would be costly and usually unnecessary. Brass scrap is remelted as brass, not copper, so less than one third of the copper recovered in the US is pure metal, and over 90% of secondary aluminium is recovered as alloys.
  2. Sorting comes first. Alloys can be recycled as alloys only if scrap is sorted by composition before melting; standard scrap grades simplify the trade. Home scrap, of known composition, needs no sorting; obsolete scrap is mixed.
  3. Tramp elements. Cu (from automotive wiring) and Sn (from tinplate) are very harmful in steel. Both are nobler than Fe, so they are not oxidised into the slag during refining; once dissolved they stay in the melt and build up with each recycling cycle. Cu causes hot shortness, cracking during hot rolling.
  4. Remedies: better scrap sorting to keep Cu and Sn out; where build-up has occurred, dilution with uncontaminated primary metal; otherwise down-cycling, for example automotive steel to rebar.
  5. Tolerance depends on the base metal. Very low Sn harms steel, but copper alloys tolerate far more Sn, so each scrap should go where its impurities do no harm.
  6. Aluminium scrap: Al is more reactive than Fe, Si, Cu and Zn, so these cannot be oxidised out; only a few elements (chiefly Mg, by chlorination) can be removed. Sorting is even more critical.
  7. Complex and hazardous scrap: a smartphone holds over 60 elements in traces, so separation is costly; Hg, Cd and flame retardants need expensive off-gas treatment.
pts: Alloys are recycled as alloys because pure metal is costly and unnecessary: brass as brass, less than one third of US recovered Cu as pure metal, over 90% of secondary Al as alloys
Sorting by composition before melting and standard scrap grades; home scrap needs none, obsolete scrap is mixed
Tramp elements Cu and Sn in steel, from wiring and tinplate; Cu gives hot shortness during hot rolling
Explains that Cu and Sn are nobler than Fe, so not oxidised into the slag, and build up over repeated cycles
Remedies: better sorting, dilution with primary metal, or down-cycling (automotive steel to rebar)
Tolerance depends on the base metal: Sn harmful in steel, tolerated in copper alloys
Aluminium: Fe, Si, Cu, Zn cannot be removed by oxidation (only a few, chiefly Mg by chlorination), so sorting is critical
Complexity of modern products (smartphone over 60 elements) and hazardous materials (Hg, Cd, flame retardants) that need off-gas treatment

5c.watch:
• "Discuss" wants the reason behind each factor. For tramp elements the key reason is thermodynamic: oxidising refining moves to the slag mainly the elements whose oxides are more stable than FeO (Si, Mn, Al, Ti; P only under a basic slag), so Cu, Sn, Ni and Mo stay.
  • Hot shortness: during reheating, Fe oxidises at the surface while Cu does not, so a Cu-rich film forms under the scale. It melts at about 1083 degrees C (lower with Sn) and penetrates the grain boundaries.
  • Do not answer with the scrap classification alone; the factors are metallurgical (composition, refining, contamination), not commercial.

6a.html:
Classification of crushers

Crushing is done in stages, each with its own type of machine:

  1. Primary (coarse) crushers take run-of-mine ore (up to about 1500 mm) and reduce it to a size the next crusher can take.
    • Jaw crushers: the Blake crusher (swing jaw pivoted at the top, largest movement at the bottom, so it seldom chokes) and the Dodge crusher (pivoted at the bottom, many fines, tends to choke).
    • Gyratory crushers: a conical head gyrating inside a fixed concave; continuous discharge, high capacity.
  2. Secondary (intermediate) crushers take the primary product and prepare feed for grinding.
    • Modified gyratories: the cone crusher (faster, for smaller pieces).
    • Roll crushers: smooth rolls (compression only) and toothed rolls (compression, impact and shear).
    • Stamp mills: mechanical mortar and pestle.

Definitions

  • Mouth: the point at which rock enters the crusher.
  • Gape: the opening of the mouth, measured at right angles to the fixed jaw. It fixes the largest piece that will enter, and it is quoted first in the crusher size: a 66 x 84 crusher has a 66 in gape and an 84 in jaw width.
  • Stroke (throw): the difference between the open and closed positions of the swing jaw, measured at the throat (the discharge point). A short throw is used for brittle rock (quartz), a long throw for tough rock that deforms without breaking.
pts: Classifies crushers by stage: primary (coarse) and secondary (intermediate)
Primary examples: jaw crusher and gyratory crusher
Distinguishes Blake (pivot at top) and Dodge (pivot at bottom) jaw crushers
Secondary examples: cone crusher, smooth and toothed roll crushers (or stamp mill)
Defines mouth as the point at which rock enters the crusher
Defines gape as the opening at the mouth (at right angles to the fixed jaw), which fixes the largest piece; size quoted as gape x width (66 x 84)
Defines stroke (throw) as the difference between the open and closed openings at the throat

  • Do not confuse the stroke with the set: the set is the opening at the throat (the product size), the stroke is how much that opening changes.
  • Tumbling mills (rod, ball, autogenous) are grinding machines, not crushers; mention them only as the next stage.

6b.html:
Similarities. Both are primary compression crushers lined with manganese steel; a gyratory crusher is like a jaw crusher with circular jaws. Reduction ratio and power per tonne at equal capacity are about the same.

Differences

FeatureJaw crusherGyratory crusher
Crushing surfacestwo flat jaws in a V; one fixed, one swingingconical head gyrating inside a fixed concave
Action and dischargeintermittent: crushes only as the jaw closescontinuous: some part of the head always crushing
Power draftuneven; flywheels needednearly uniform
Speed250 to 400 strokes per min125 to 425 gyrations per min
Strokelongershorter (nip 21 to 23 degrees)
Capacitylowermuch greater for the same feed (up to 4500 t/h)
Maintenancemoreless
Suited tosmall plants; clayey or fibrous rocklarge tonnages; flat slabs cannot slip through

Conclusion: the gyratory is preferred for large tonnages; the jaw crusher for small plants and sticky feed.

6c.html:
Angle of nip. In a smooth roll crusher a particle is drawn in ("nipped") between the two rolls only if it meets them at a small enough angle. The angle of nip is the angle between the tangents to the two roll faces at the points where the particle touches them, 2\alpha. It fixes the largest particle that rolls of a given diameter can take.

Derivation. Rolls of radius R turn toward each other with a gap d (the product size); a spherical particle of radius r rests on them, touching each roll at one point.

Step 1, geometry. The line from a roll centre to the particle centre passes through the contact point and has length R + r. Its horizontal projection is the distance from the roll centre to the mid-plane, R + d/2. With \alpha the angle this line makes with the line of roll centres:

\boxed{\cos\alpha = \frac{R + d/2}{R + r}}

The tangent at the contact is perpendicular to this line, so it makes the angle \alpha with the vertical. The two tangents meet below the particle at 2\alpha, the angle of nip.

Step 2, forces. At each contact the roll exerts

  • a normal force N along the radius, whose vertical component N\sin\alpha pushes the particle up, out of the rolls;
  • a friction force \mu N along the tangent, dragged downward by the turning roll, whose vertical component \mu N\cos\alpha pulls the particle down.

Step 3, condition for nipping (weight neglected):

\mu N\cos\alpha \geq N\sin\alpha \quad\Rightarrow\quad \boxed{\tan\alpha \leq \mu}

The largest angle of nip is 2\alpha_{max} = 2\arctan\mu; for steel rolls on rock, \mu \approx 0.29 gives about 32^\circ.

Useful forms. Largest particle nipped: r_{max} = (R + d/2)/\cos\alpha - R. Roll radius needed: R = (r\cos\alpha - d/2)/(1 - \cos\alpha).

Example: 600 mm rolls (R = 300 mm), gap 12 mm, \mu = 0.29: \alpha = 16.2^\circ, \cos\alpha = 0.9604,

r_{max} = \frac{306}{0.9604} - 300 = 18.6\ \mathrm{mm}

so the largest feed is about 37.2 mm, a reduction ratio of only about 3.1. Smooth rolls must therefore be large in diameter, and they give small reduction ratios.
pts: Defines the angle of nip as the angle between the tangents to the roll faces at the contact points (2\alpha; or \alpha, if that convention is stated), which limits the particle size that can be nipped
Labelled sketch with R, r, gap d, the angle \alpha, and the forces N and \mu N
Geometry: \cos\alpha = (R + d/2)/(R + r), with the reason (centre-line length R + r, horizontal projection R + d/2)
Resolves the forces: upward component N\sin\alpha of the normal force against downward component \mu N\cos\alpha of friction
Condition \tan\alpha \leq \mu, maximum angle of nip 2\arctan\mu \approx 32^\circ for \mu \approx 0.29
Rearranged form for the largest feed or the roll radius
A worked number (for example 600 mm rolls with a 12 mm gap nip particles up to about 37 mm) or the conclusion that smooth rolls need large diameters and give small reduction ratios

7a.html:
A ball mill is a cylinder turning about a horizontal axis, charged with ore and hard steel or ceramic balls (30 to 50% of its volume). The printed "change" is read as charge.

Lifting and falling. As the shell rotates, friction and the lifters carry the charge up the rising side of the lining. Near the shoulder, centrifugal action neutralises the weight. Higher up, gravity wins and the balls leave the lining: the outer ones fly in free parabolic paths (cataracting), the inner ones roll down the sloping surface (cascading). They land on the toe of the charge at the bottom of the falling side and are carried round again.

Zones of the charge

  • Zone A (against the lining, rising side): most of the charge is lifted with the shell, but some particles move the opposite way (shearing). Reduction by abrasion and impact.
  • Zone B (the tumbling surface): particles move with their neighbours but are in intimate contact and tumble over each other: the major grinding zone, by abrasion and impact.
  • Zone C (impact zone, the toe): particles that have fallen from the opposite side strike the charge; reduction solely by impact.
  • Free fall: no significant contact between particles, so no grinding until the toe is reached.

Effect of speed. The critical speed, at which a ball is just held to the shell for a full turn (Mg = 2Mv^2/D), is

N_c = \frac{42.3}{\sqrt{D}}\ \mathrm{rpm}\quad (D\ \text{in m})
  • Too slow: the balls only roll down (cascading); limited grinding by abrasion.
  • At or above N_c: the charge centrifuges and sticks to the shell; hardly any grinding.
  • Normal: 65 to 82% of N_c, so balls are thrown onto the toe; a 2 m mill (N_c = 29.9 rpm) runs at about 19 to 25 rpm.

Other factors. Profiled liners increase lifting at a given speed; they reduce shearing but increase the vigorous reduction in zone B. The amount of charge sets the share of particles in each zone. Falling balls must strike the charge, not the liner, or liner wear rises sharply.
pts: Neat labelled sketch: shell, rotation direction, charge with shoulder and toe, trajectories and zones
Charge lifted up the lining and falling back under gravity: cataracting paths to the toe and cascading down the surface
Zone A: lifted with the shell, some shearing, abrasion and impact
Zone B: tumbling in intimate contact, the major grinding zone
Zone C: impact zone at the toe, reduction solely by impact
No grinding during free fall because particles do not touch
Critical speed defined with N_c = 42.3/\sqrt{D} rpm, and the effect of running too slow (cascading) or too fast (centrifuging)
Normal operation at 65 to 82% of N_c with 30 to 50% filling
Effect of liners or the need for balls to land on the charge, not the liner

7b.html:
Recovery is the percentage of the total metal contained in the ore that is recovered in the concentrate:

R = \frac{\text{metal in concentrate}}{\text{metal in feed}}\times 100 = \frac{Cc}{Ff}\times 100

A recovery of 90% means 90% of the metal reports to the concentrate and 10% is lost in the tailing.

Ratio of concentration is the weight of feed (heads) needed to make one unit weight of concentrate:

K = \frac{F}{C} = \frac{c - t}{f - t}

1 t of concentrate from 20 t of ore is a ratio of 20 to 1.

The two are independent and both are needed to judge an operation: hand-picking a few lumps of pure galena gives a high ratio but a very low recovery, and not concentrating at all gives 100% recovery at a ratio of 1.
pts: Recovery: percentage of the metal in the feed that is recovered in the concentrate, Cc/Ff \times 100
Ratio of concentration: weight of feed per unit weight of concentrate, F/C, with an example such as 20 to 1
The assay form (c - t)/(f - t) or c(f - t)/[f(c - t)] \times 100, or the 90% recovery example
Notes that the two are independent and both are needed (galena hand-picking example)

7c.fix: • Slide 17 of the Particle selection deck (and Example 3.1 of the reading, page 7) writes the denominator of the recovery as 0.21 \times 2000. The head assay is 2.1%, so it must be 0.021 \times 2000 = 42 g of Pb; the printed result, 91.83%, is correct only with 0.021.
7c.html:
Given: head F = 2000 g at f = 2.1\% Pb; concentrate C = 70 g at c = 55.1\% Pb; tailing assay t = 0.1\% Pb.

Find: the ratio of concentration and the recovery.

Step 1, ratio of concentration (from the weights):

K = \frac{\text{weight of heads}}{\text{weight of concentrate}} = \frac{2000\ \mathrm{g}}{70\ \mathrm{g}} = 28.6

Step 2, lead in each stream:

\begin{aligned} \text{Pb in concentrate} &= Cc = 70 \times 0.551 = 38.57\ \mathrm{g} \\ \text{Pb in head} &= Ff = 2000 \times 0.021 = 42.0\ \mathrm{g} \end{aligned}

Step 3, recovery:

R = \frac{Cc}{Ff}\times 100 = \frac{38.57}{42.0}\times 100 = 91.8\%

Alternative, from assays only (two-product formula, using the tailing assay):

\begin{aligned} K &= \frac{c - t}{f - t} = \frac{0.551 - 0.001}{0.021 - 0.001} = 27.5 \\ R &= \frac{c(f - t)}{f(c - t)}\times 100 = \frac{0.551 \times 0.020}{0.021 \times 0.550}\times 100 = 95.4\% \end{aligned}

The difference comes from errors in sampling and weighing.

Answer: ratio of concentration = 28.6 to 1; recovery = 91.8% (by assays alone, 27.5 to 1 and 95.4%).
pts: Ratio of concentration as weight of heads over weight of concentrate (or (c - t)/(f - t))
K = 2000/70 = 28.6 to 1 (or 27.5 to 1 from the assay formula)
Recovery as metal in the concentrate over metal in the head, Cc/Ff \times 100 (or c(f - t)/[f(c - t)] \times 100)
Lead in the concentrate 38.57 g and in the head 42.0 g (or the assay differences 0.020 and 0.550)
Recovery = 38.57/42.0 \times 100 = 91.8\% (or 95.4% from the two-product formula)

8b.html:
Given: 30% galena, 40% quartz, 30% water by weight; specific gravity galena 7.5, quartz 2.7, water 1.0.

Find: pulp dilution, pulp density and percent solids.

Basis: 100 g of pulp: 30 g galena, 40 g quartz, 30 g water.

Step 1, volumes:

\begin{aligned} V &= \frac{30}{7.5} + \frac{40}{2.7} + \frac{30}{1.0} = 4.00 + 14.81 + 30.00 = 48.81\ \mathrm{cm^3} \end{aligned}

Step 2, pulp dilution (water to solids by weight):

D = \frac{30}{30 + 40} = 0.429

Step 3, pulp density (weight per unit volume):

d = \frac{100\ \mathrm{g}}{48.81\ \mathrm{cm^3}} = 2.05\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}

Step 4, percent solids (by weight):

\frac{70}{100}\times 100 = 70\%

Answer: pulp dilution 0.43 to 1, pulp density 2.05 (\mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}), 70% solids.
pts: States a basis of 100 g of pulp with 70 g solids and 30 g water
Volumes from specific gravities: 4.0 + 14.8 + 30.0 = 48.8 \mathrm{cm^3}
Pulp dilution 30/70 = 0.43 to 1 (water to solids by weight; 0.428 or 0.429 equally right)
Pulp density 100/48.8 = 2.05\ \mathrm{g\,cm^{-3}}
Percent solids = 70\% by weight

8c.html:
What it is. A hydrocyclone is a vertical-current classifier with no moving parts. It handles large volumes of slurry and classifies them, by particle size and/or specific gravity, into two products: an underflow (coarse, dense) and an overflow (fine, light, most of the water). It replaces gravity by centrifugal force.

Construction.

  • A conical vessel open at its apex (underflow, spigot), joined to a short cylindrical section.
  • A tangential feed inlet in the cylindrical section.
  • A top plate through which an axial overflow pipe passes; its short extension inside, the vortex finder, prevents short-circuiting of feed into the overflow.
  • Typical proportions: vortex finder about 0.35D_c, cylinder length about D_c, cone included angle 10 to 20 degrees, apex 10 to 35% of D_c.

Functioning.

  1. Slurry is pumped in under pressure through the tangential inlet and spins; cycloning starts in the feed chamber. The centrifugal force is 10 to 4000 times gravity, so settling is fast.
  2. Every particle is acted on by an outward centrifugal force and an inward drag force of the liquid flowing towards the vortex finder.
  3. Coarse and heavy particles are thrown to the wall and travel down the outer spiral to the apex as underflow.
  4. Most of the liquid leaves at the top; it drags fine and light particles to the centre and up the inner spiral into the vortex finder as overflow. An air core forms on the axis.
  5. Between the two flows lies the envelope of zero vertical velocity: particles thrown outside it leave in the underflow, those swept inside leave in the overflow.
  6. A particle on the envelope feels equal centrifugal and drag forces: this is the cut size d_{50}, with a 50% chance of either product.

Control. A smaller cyclone diameter gives a finer cut; the vortex finder and apex diameters, the feed percent solids and the inlet pressure (throughput Q \propto P^{0.5}) also set the performance. Hydrocyclones close ball-mill circuits and deslime and dewater pulps.
pts: Defines the hydrocyclone as a classifier with no moving parts that splits slurry by size and/or specific gravity into underflow and overflow by centrifugal force
Neat labelled sketch: cylindrical section, tangential inlet, cone, apex (underflow), vortex finder and overflow pipe, with flow directions
Construction details: top plate, vortex finder prevents short-circuiting (proportions such as 0.35D_c or a 10 to 20 degree cone)
Feed under pressure enters tangentially; centrifugal force 10 to 4000 g accelerates settling
Outward centrifugal force against inward drag force on each particle
Coarse and dense particles to the wall, down the outer spiral, out at the apex
Fines and most water dragged to the centre, up the inner spiral to the vortex finder; air core
Envelope of zero vertical velocity separates the two flows
Cut size d_{50} (equal forces, 50% chance) and its control by cyclone diameter, vortex finder, apex, percent solids and pressure

8c.watch:
• "Neat sketch" is worth about a fifth of the marks: label the inlet as tangential, show the vortex finder reaching below the top plate, and mark both spirals with arrows.
